newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK graft buster quits, says unrelated to handover.
newsitem.headline: HK graft buster quits, says unrelated to handover.

text.p: Hong Kong's top graft buster said on Friday he had decided to resign but added that it had no connection with China taking over the British colony next year.

"About three months ago, I told the government I didn't intend to stay on," said Michael Leung, Commissioner of the Independent Commision Against Corruption, the first ethnic Chinese to hold the post.
Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight on June 30 as a Special Administrative Region (SAR).

Leung's move sparked speculation in the local media that Hong Kong's chief executive-designate Tung Chee-hwa, who is talent-scouting for his future cabinet, disliked Leung, who has been in the top anti-corruption job for less than a year.
Some analysts said Leung's departure might be the start of an exodus of key officials before the handover.
"The government asked me a few times to stay on, and I decided after very careful consideration not to extend the contract beyond March 1997," Leung told a news conference.
"My decision is entirely personal and unrelated to the SAR government," he said. "This has nothing to do with the Chief Executive."
He added his move was unrelated to the present administration but declined to divulge the underlying reasons.

Leung said he had extended his contract, originally set to expire next Thursday, for three months, to allow the government time to hunt for a successor. He said he had faced no pressure or intervention from China during his term in office.
